title: Temperature, heat and thermodynamics
note: Temperature (in kelvin) is proportional to the average kinetic energy of particles; heat is energy that flows because of a temperature difference. The first law, ΔU = Q − W (W is work done by the system), is energy conservation. The second law says entropy of an isolated system never decreases, which limits every heat engine below 100% efficiency.

read.title: Heat, work, and the arrow of time
text: Temperature and heat are often confused. Temperature tracks how fast particles jiggle: for an ideal gas, the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT, with T in kelvin. Heat is energy in transit from a hotter object to a colder one. Adding heat usually raises temperature by Q = mcΔT, but during melting or boiling the energy goes into breaking bonds and the temperature holds steady.

The first law of thermodynamics is conservation of energy for thermal systems. The change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added minus the work the system does. A gas that expands against a piston does work and cools unless heat flows in to replace the energy.

The second law is different in kind. Heat flows on its own only from hot to cold, and the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. One consequence is that no heat engine can turn all of its input heat into work; some must be dumped into a colder reservoir. The best possible efficiency, the Carnot limit, is 1 − T_c/T_h. An engine running between 600 K and 300 K can never exceed 50% efficiency, no matter how cleverly it is built.
